newsitem.title: USA: NBC says it reached settlement with Jewell.
newsitem.headline: NBC says it reached settlement with Jewell.

text.p: NBC, which reported that security guard Richard Jewell was close to arrest for allegedly planting a bomb at last July's Atlanta Olympics, reached a settlement with him on Monday to avert a threatened libel suit, Jewell's lawyers said.

The network, in a terse one paragraph sentence, said only that it had resolved its differences with Jewell "after a vigorous and thoughtful exchange of views in which both sides defended the correctness of their positions."
A source close to the negotiations told Reuters that NBC agreed to pay Jewell an undisclosed financial settlement.
Jewell's lawyer Lin Wood said, "We are satisfied with the settlement and are obviously very pleased to settle without going into a lawsuit. I'm sure NBC will characterise this also as satisfactory."

Jewell was an AT&T security guard who discovered a mysterious bag at Centennial Olympic Park on July 27 and helped get people away from the scene before a pipe bomb in it exploded, killing two people and injuring 100 others.
While he maintained his innocence, several news organisations reported that Jewell was a chief suspect including NBC, which was broadcasting the Olympics live in the United States.

After 4 1/2 months in which his life was turned upside down, Jewell was finally cleared by the Justice Department of any involvement in the bombing in late October and has since threatened to sue several news organisations and the FBI for libelling him.

Shortly after the bombing, NBC's anchorman Tom Brokaw reported, "The speculation is that the FBI is close to 'making the case' in their language. They probably have enough to arrest him right now, probably enough to prosecute him, but you always want to have enough to convict him as well. There are still holes in this case."
In an interview with CBS's "60 Minutes" in September, Brokaw said he based his report on information provided by knowledgeable sources in law enforcement agencies in Washington and Atlanta.
Wood said lawsuits were still being considered against the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, which broke the story that Jewell was a suspect, and two FBI agents who questioned him.

Wood added, "We are going to be suing them (the Journal-Constitution) in a couple of weeks and have not entered into any settlement discussions (because) the newspaper continues to stand proudly behind their coverage as accurate. We will sue."

Jewell's attorneys said they have twice unsuccessfully asked the newspaper for retractions. Wood said Jewell was considering suing the FBI because, "We feel they violated Richard Jewell's civil rights, but we're not jumping out yet to file the suit. We want to look and see who else did anything or knew anything or acquiesced in the agency."

Meanwhile, the FBI on Monday made public a telephone warning received shortly before the pipe bomb went and offered a reward of up to $500,000 for information leading to the arrest of the bomber or bombers.
